opus-5.5.text:
I think it's important to separate out the different things that make clinical trials slow, because AI helps with some of them a lot more than others.

Some of the slowness is irreducible, at least in the short term. If you're testing whether a drug extends life or prevents a disease that develops over years, there's a biological clock on that, and no amount of intelligence makes the patients' bodies move faster. You still have to observe what happens. So I don't think we go from ten years to ten days.

But a surprising amount of the time isn't that. It's things like designing the trial, recruiting the right patients, the back-and-forth on paperwork and regulatory submissions, running sites, cleaning and analyzing data. A lot of that is essentially cognitive and administrative labor, and that's exactly where powerful AI should compress things enormously.

And then there's a deeper effect that I think matters more. Right now a lot of trials fail, and they fail because we went in with a weak understanding of the biology. We picked the wrong target, the wrong patient population, the wrong dose. If AI systems help us actually understand the mechanism much better before we ever get to humans, through better models of biology, better biomarkers, better ways of measuring whether something is working early on, then you run fewer trials that were doomed from the start, and the ones you run are cleaner and smaller and give you clear answers faster.

I'd point to the COVID vaccines as an existence proof. When there was enormous urgency and the science was well understood, we got from sequence to authorization in about a year, while doing it safely. That tells you a lot of the normal timeline is not fundamental.

So my rough view is that the whole pipeline, discovery through approval, could compress by something like a factor of several, maybe up to ten in the best cases, rather than by a factor of a thousand. And that's where I got the idea of compressing maybe fifty to a hundred years of biological progress into five or ten. Not because any single trial becomes instant, but because you're running many more good experiments in parallel and wasting far less time on bad ones. The limiting factors become physical and institutional, and we'd need regulators to adapt as well, which I think is possible if the evidence is strong.

r001.rationale: The response says many trials fail because researchers choose the wrong target, patient population, or dose. It does not state that most fail because the drug lacks efficacy.

r002.rationale: The response says some trial timelines are constrained by biology and observation, and that AI will compress timelines by a factor of several rather than a thousand.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where people's intuitions are most miscalibrated, in both directions actually. There's a camp that says, look, AI can design the molecule in an afternoon, so we'll have cures for everything in two years. And then there's a camp that says, the biology is the biology, the trial takes the time it takes, you can't speed up a human body, so none of this matters much. I think both of those are wrong, and the truth is more interesting.

Let me start with the thing that's genuinely rate-limiting. A Phase 3 trial, you're often following patients for a year, two years, sometimes longer for something like a cardiovascular outcome or an Alzheimer's progression endpoint. You can't compress the calendar time it takes for a disease to progress or not progress in a human being. That's real. AI doesn't change that directly.

But when you actually look at where the time goes in drug development, the thing that surprised me is how little of it is that irreducible biological clock. An enormous fraction is what I'd call institutional and informational latency. It's months to write the protocol. It's months of back-and-forth with regulators. It's often a year or more just to recruit patients, because you're trying to find the right people across hundreds of sites and the data about who's eligible is sitting in messy records nobody has read. Trials fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the drug, because the endpoint was chosen badly or the dose was wrong or the population was too heterogeneous. And then the analysis, the writing of the submission, the regulatory review. A lot of this is thousands of smart people doing careful but slow cognitive work, and that is exactly the thing that a very capable AI, something I've described as a country of geniuses in a datacenter, can do much faster.

So my picture is something like this. You have these systems acting as, essentially, principal investigators and biostatisticians and regulatory writers, running in parallel. They design much better trials to begin with, so you waste fewer years on failures. They identify eligible patients far faster. They can run adaptive designs that would be too complicated for a human team to manage, where you're learning as you go and reallocating. They write the regulatory submission in a week instead of a year. And critically, they can look at the enormous backlog of existing trial data and real-world evidence, and squeeze a lot more inference out of it, so you need smaller or shorter confirmatory trials to be confident.

And then there's the second-order thing, which is that the biology clock itself isn't totally fixed either. We rely on long-duration trials partly because we don't have good biomarkers. If the AI helps us discover a surrogate endpoint that reliably predicts the long-term outcome at six months instead of three years, you've just cut the trial dramatically. That's happened before with human science, it's just slow. And a lot of safety signal detection could move earlier if you had much better models of toxicity. So I think things like organoids, better animal models or replacements for them, in silico prediction, those start eating into the part that seems irreducible.

The honest caveat is the regulatory and social side. The FDA, and regulators everywhere, are appropriately conservative, and I think they should be. There's going to be a period where the AI could move faster than the institutions are willing to let it, and that friction is going to be the real bottleneck, not the science. I actually spend a fair amount of time thinking about how you get regulators to a place where they can trust and verify what these systems are doing, because if we don't solve that, we leave a lot of the gains on the table.

So if you force me to put numbers on it, and I want to be upfront that these are guesses, I think something that today takes ten to twelve years from target to approval could plausibly become two to three years for a lot of indications, and that's not a speculative far-future thing, I think that's within the sort of five-to-ten year window after you have these very powerful systems. Not because we've abolished the human body's timeline, but because we've taken out all the dead time around it, and we've gotten better at not running the wrong trial in the first place. And when you compound that across the whole pipeline, across all the diseases at once, that's how you get to the picture I talked about of compressing fifty or a hundred years of biomedical progress into a decade. It's not one miracle. It's a lot of friction coming out of a system that was never really optimized for speed.

r001.rationale: The response says trials can fail because of poor endpoints, incorrect doses, or heterogeneous populations; it does not say most fail because the drug lacks efficacy.

r002.rationale: The response says AI cannot directly compress the time a disease takes to progress in patients and that long-term trials retain a biological time limit.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different things here. One is how quickly you can design a treatment, and the other is how quickly you can find out whether it actually works in humans. AI could compress the first enormously. The second has some constraints that are harder to get around.

If you need to know whether a drug prevents a disease over five years, making the researchers a hundred times smarter doesn’t automatically turn that into a two-week experiment. You still need to observe what happens. And you need to catch side effects that you didn’t anticipate.

But I wouldn’t assume that today’s trial timelines are some fundamental limit, either. Better patient selection, better trial design, better measurements of whether a treatment is working—all of those could help. You might also arrive at clinical trials with candidates that are much more likely to succeed, which would make the whole process faster even if an individual trial still takes a while.

So I’d expect substantial acceleration, but uneven acceleration. Some things could move very quickly; others will still be limited by the time it takes biology to reveal the answer.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that most clinical trials fail because the drug lacks efficacy.

r002.rationale: It says AI cannot make a five-year outcome trial into a two-week experiment and that biology still limits how quickly results emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on which part of the process you mean. AI could make designing a trial, recruiting patients, and analyzing the results much faster. It could also help us choose better candidates in the first place, so that fewer trials fail.

But there’s a part you can’t simply speed up by thinking faster. If you need to know whether a treatment prevents a disease over several years, or whether a side effect appears after a year, there’s a biological clock involved. You have to wait, unless you’ve developed a reliable way to predict those outcomes earlier.

So I’m optimistic about substantial acceleration, but I wouldn’t assume clinical trials suddenly happen instantaneously. The question is how much of the delay is logistics and uncertainty that intelligence can remove, and how much is genuinely waiting for biology.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI could help choose better candidates so fewer trials fail, but does not state that most trials fail because the drug lacks efficacy.

r002.rationale: It says trials cannot be made instantaneous because some outcomes require waiting for biological effects over time, unless those outcomes can be reliably predicted earlier.
